headline: The Boulders Still Hold: Bass Working the Skinny Water Off the Point
subhead: Mid-July has settled into its rhythm at Montauk — resident bass on the rips, jumbo blues crashing bait, and the first bluefin showing south of the Light.
body_markdown:
There's a specific quiet that settles over the Point in mid-July. The spring run is long gone, the crowds have thinned from what they were in May, and what's left is the real fishery — the one that doesn't need a blitz to prove itself. I stood on the boulder field below the Lighthouse at 5:15 this morning, watching the tide build against the rocks, and that's Montauk in July. Not chaos. Just the same current doing what it's done for ten thousand years, and the bass knowing exactly where to sit in it.

Water's reading around 70 degrees off the Point right now, which is right where you want it for this stretch of summer — warm enough to keep the bait moving, cool enough that the resident bass haven't gone deep and sour on us. I'm still finding stripers stacked on the down-current side of the boulder fields between North Bar and the Lighthouse, holding tight to structure the way they always do when the tide is really moving. The pattern hasn't changed in twenty years and it's not going to change this week: cast a bucktail — I've been throwing 1.5-ounce white and olive — across the seam where the fast water meets the eddy, let it sink clean off the edge, and work it back slow along the bottom. Don't rip it. These fish aren't chasing, they're ambushing, and a bucktail that swims too fast right past a rock just gets ignored. Slot fish in the 28-34 inch range have been the bread and butter, with the occasional overslot pushing 20 pounds coming off the deeper water east of Shagwong Reef on the last two hours of the incoming.

Shagwong itself has been holding better than North Bar most mornings this week — I think it's the extra depth keeping bait around longer into the day. Turtle Cove has been quieter, more of an evening spot right now, best worked right at last light when the bass slide up onto the shallower rock to feed before full dark. If you're throwing topwater or a big pencil popper, that's your window. I had one push a foot-long swirl at a black Gibbs popper off Turtle Cove Tuesday evening that I still think about.

Bluefish have been the wild card, and not in a bad way — these aren't snappers, they're jumbos, 8 to 12 pounds, showing up mixed in with the bass on the same current edges and absolutely wrecking anything metal you throw at them. If you want bass and don't want your leader shredded, downsize your wire or just accept you're going to lose a few bucktails. I've been running 40-pound fluorocarbon instead of straight mono on the bucktail rigs just to survive the blitzes when the blues move in.

South side, the fluke drift off Frisbie's and down toward Camp Hero has been steady, not spectacular — that's the honest read. Boats working 25 to 35 feet of water on the outgoing have been picking at keepers in the 19 to 22 inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow, with a lot of shorts mixed in that need to go back. Nobody's filling a cooler in an afternoon right now, but if you're patient and willing to cover ground, there's a decent fish for dinner most trips. Weakfish have been scattered and incidental — a few coming up mixed in with the fluke drift, nothing to plan a trip around yet.

The thing that's got the harbor talking this week is what's happening offshore of the Point. Bluefin have pushed south into range for the smaller center consoles, and I know a handful of guys who got their first tuna of the year in the last week without running much past the 20-fathom curve. That's early and it's worth paying attention to — if that bluefin push holds and doesn't slide back east, it could be a real midsummer bite developing close enough to fish in a half-day window, which almost never happens this early.

Here's what I'm watching for the week ahead. There's squid building up around the Rhode Island and Nantucket side of the Sound right now, and historically when that squid bio-mass starts pushing this direction, it's exactly the kind of forage event that turns the Montauk rips from a good pattern into a serious one — bigger bass, more consistent current-edge feeding, the kind of setup that gets guys eeling at night off the Lighthouse rocks again. It hasn't arrived yet. If it does slide west into Block Island Sound over the next week or two, I'd shift time to the evening tide at Shagwong and start soaking eels after dark. If it stalls out east, the bucktail-on-the-boulders pattern we've got right now is still a legitimate way to spend a morning — just don't expect every drift to produce. Cover water, work the seams, and let the rock do what the rock has always done out here.
